record.paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
record.original_question: How should future peer-to-peer protocols for data sharing be designed so that adversaries cannot easily construct denial-of-service attacks by exploiting loosely constrained protocol features such as unconstrained responses, routing behavior, or resource allocation rules?

evidence.quote: In the future, P2P protocols need to be designed to make it hard for adversaries to construct DoS attacks by taking advantage of loosely constrained protocol features.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a peer-to-peer (P2P) data-sharing system modeled as a dynamic network of autonomous nodes that interact according to a protocol P. The protocol P specifies, for each node, (i) how it responds to incoming messages (response rules), (ii) how it forwards or routes queries and data (routing rules), and (iii) how it allocates local resources such as bandwidth, storage, and CPU to handle requests (resource allocation rules). A denial-of-service (DoS) attack is a strategy executed by a bounded coalition A of adversarial nodes (with |A| small relative to the total population) whose goal is to cause a disproportionate degradation of service availability for honest participants — formally, to drive some measurable performance metric (e.g., query success rate, average response latency, or fraction of reachable honest peers) below a chosen threshold while expending only o(1) of the resources required from the attacker compared to the damage inflicted on the system.

Say that a protocol feature is "loosely constrained" if it permits a node, upon receiving a single message of size s, to be obligated (by the protocol rules) to generate responses, forwarded traffic, or resource commitments whose total cost is ω(s), or if it permits an adversary to trigger arbitrarily many such actions without supplying a commensurate proof of work, identity, or prior interaction.

Problem. Design a P2P data-sharing protocol P satisfying the following properties simultaneously:

(1) Correctness/efficiency in the honest setting: with all nodes following P, the system supports data lookup, storage, and retrieval with polylogarithmic per-operation cost in the number of nodes.

(2) DoS resistance: for every adversarial coalition A of size at most a constant fraction ε of the network and every strategy A may follow within the syntactic rules of P, the ratio (damage inflicted on honest peers) / (resources expended by A) is bounded by a constant, where damage and resources are measured in a uniform cost model covering bandwidth, computation, and memory.

(3) No loosely constrained features: every response rule, routing rule, and resource-allocation rule of P must be tightly constrained in the sense above — i.e., the work induced on any honest node by a single adversarial message of size s is O(s), up to amortization by verifiable proofs.

Provide such a protocol together with a proof of its DoS resistance, or prove that no protocol can satisfy (1)–(3) simultaneously under standard cryptographic assumptions.
artifact.status_search_result: DoS resistance in peer-to-peer overlays remains an active research area with many partial mitigations (proof-of-work, admission control, secure routing in DHTs, rate limiting, reputation systems), but no general protocol design is known that simultaneously achieves polylogarithmic efficiency and provable constant-ratio DoS resistance against a constant fraction of adversaries while eliminating all loosely constrained features. The problem is generally regarded as open in the P2P security literature.

status_evidence.title: Surveys on P2P security and DoS attacks
status_evidence.snippet: Studies of DoS amplification in DHTs and overlays continue to identify exploitable, loosely constrained protocol behaviors, with proposed mitigations being partial.
status_evidence.claim: DoS resistance in P2P protocols is an ongoing open design problem with only partial solutions.
